title: Reflections on the Early Days of Reserve Management Purchases and the Maintenance of Ample Reserves

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: SOMA Manager Roberto Perli delivered a technical briefing on the Federal Reserve's transition from abundant to ample reserves, including the October 2025 decision to end balance sheet runoff and the December 2025 initiation of Reserve Management Purchases (RMPs). The speech documents a notable tightening in money market conditions through late 2025, characterized by declining ON RRP usage to de minimis levels, rising repo rates above IORB, increased repo rate volatility, and more frequent usage of Standing Repo Facilities (SRPs). Perli outlines the six indicators the Fed monitors to assess reserve adequacy and explains the mechanics of how ample reserves differ from abundant or scarce regimes in terms of rate sensitivity.
key_points: At its October 2025 meeting, the FOMC decided to conclude the runoff of aggregate SOMA securities holdings effective December 1, 2025
The FOMC instructed the Desk to begin RMPs in December 2025 when it judged reserves had declined to the ample range
In the ample reserves regime, the federal funds rate is only modestly sensitive to short-term variations in reserve supply, unlike scarce reserves where it is highly sensitive
By October 2025, ON RRP usage had declined to de minimis levels, reducing the pool of funds available to shift into private repo and causing repo rates to rise above IORB
EFFR rose from approximately 7 basis points below IORB in mid-September to approximately 1 basis point below IORB by November 2025
SRP usage became larger and more frequent as repo market conditions tightened through late 2025

Federal Home Loan Banks (FHLBs) played a key connecting role between repo and federal funds markets, shifting lending from federal funds to repo and leveraging higher repo rates to negotiate higher federal funds rates
TGA rebuild after the debt limit increase in early July 2025 contributed to reducing system liquidity to the lowest levels since balance sheet runoff began
Perli emphasized that not all reserve adequacy indicators need to move simultaneously to conclude reserves are entering the ample range; some indicators move sooner than others
why_it_matters: This speech provides authoritative insight into the Federal Reserve's operational framework for managing reserve conditions in the ample reserves regime. Understanding how the Fed defines and monitors reserve adequacy is critical for market participants because it directly affects repo market functioning, the federal funds rate, and the broader transmission of monetary policy. The documented transition from abundant to ample reserves in late 2025 provides a template for how market conditions may evolve as the Fed continues its current framework. The speech also clarifies the role of RMPs as a maintenance tool rather than an easing measure, and explains when SRPs are expected to see increased usage.
market_structure_context: This speech is primarily about market structure, detailing the mechanics of the Fed's ample reserves framework. Key structural elements include: (1) The distinction between abundant, ample, and scarce reserve regimes and how each affects rate sensitivity; (2) The six indicators monitored for reserve adequacy including EFFR-IORB spread, repo reference rate deviations, ON RRP usage, SRP usage, bank borrowing levels, and intraday payment timing; (3) The role of RMPs in maintaining reserves within the ample range without actively managing the federal funds rate; (4) The mechanics of SRPs as a backstop for repo rate volatility; (5) The interaction between TGA dynamics, system liquidity, and money market rates; (6) The FHLB's role as a bridge between repo and federal funds markets. The speech documents how the transition from abundant to ample reserves in late 2025 manifested in observable market changes.
important_numbers: 2025-10: FOMC decided to end balance sheet runoff (effective December 1, 2025)
2025-12: RMPs began when reserves entered the ample range
EFFR approximately 7 bps below IORB in mid-September 2025
EFFR approximately 1 bp below IORB by November 2025
Q1 2019: benchmark levels for repo rate above IORB share and late bank payments
ON RRP declined to de minimis by October 2025
